card.hook: This isn't one building, it's a whole cluster of courtyards, passages and long façades about 300 metres across, and students wander through it all day. That's handy for you, because they make great scale in your photos.
card.stand_here: Step into the Grand Courtyard of Vilnius University, stand right at the subject, and face St John's Church facade and bell tower. The arcaded courtyard frames the church, and the observatory tower with its zodiac frieze is in view too.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view, then go to zoom 0.5x if you're close and want the whole façade or courtyard in one shot. Use zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pull in doorways, windows and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest wall, then slide to darker so the pale stonework keeps its texture and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people, and a soft overcast day suits the walls well. For the Grand Courtyard, mid-morning is a good bet.
card.selfie_here: Stand inside the Grand Courtyard with the observatory tower and its zodiac frieze behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more tower in, and hold the phone level. The courtyard is largely enclosed, so its soft midday light avoids harsh shadows on your face.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand inside the Grand Courtyard facing east, so St John's Church is on their left and its bell tower on their right, with you in the middle of the courtyard.
card.rules_and_safety: Visitors pay a small admission fee to walk the courtyards, and access can change, so check the university's current opening rules. It's a working university, so respect any signs. Stay on pavements and maintained paths for your shot.
card.challenge: Catch a student walking through an archway at the edge of your frame, so the building looks as big as it feels.
card.good_to_know: Vilnius University was founded in 1579 as the Jesuit Academy of Vilnius by Stephen Báthory. It closed after the failed November Uprising of 1830–1831 and didn't reopen until 1919. Today more than 23,000 students study here, and it also runs a library, a museum and botanical gardens.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Step into the Grand Courtyard of Vilnius University, stand right at the subject, and face St John's Church facade and bell tower. The arcaded courtyard frames the church, and the observatory tower with its zodiac frieze is in view too.

card.hook: Picture a short, sturdy brick tower sitting on a hill, with the whole Old Town's rooftops spread out below it. That's Gediminas' Tower, and it's even been on the old litas currency.
card.stand_here: Stand right at Gediminas' Tower on top of Gediminas Hill: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the walls for close shots, then step back along the hilltop to fit the whole tower in.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for close shots looking up at the tower, and 1x for the tower with some sky around it. From the platform, try zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pick out Old Town roofs and towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the tower's straight vertical edges with the vertical grid lines, and don't tilt the phone too far when shooting upwards or the walls will lean in.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening usually gives softer, warmer light on the brick. The tower houses a museum, so check the official site before you go for access to the tower and viewing platform.
card.selfie_here: Head to the green slopes of Gediminas Hill just below the tower. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low, and put the tower behind you with the Old Town and city skyline around it.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a little lower on the hill path and shoot upwards, while you stand on the green slope below the tower so the whole tower fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The climb up can be slippery after rain or snow, so wear sturdy shoes.
card.challenge: From the platform, get old Vilnius and the modern business district into one frame, then show it to a friend and ask them to guess which is which.
card.good_to_know: The first brick castle here was finished in 1409 under Grand Duke Vytautas, and the tower you see today was rebuilt in 1933. It's a symbol of both Vilnius and Lithuania, and the national flag was raised on it again on 7 October 1988.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at Gediminas' Tower on top of Gediminas Hill: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the walls for close shots, then step back along the hilltop to fit the whole tower in.

card.hook: Picture a bronze angel blowing a trumpet over a café square, in a neighbourhood that declared itself a republic on 1 April 1997. Welcome to Užupis, where the joke stuck and nobody minds.
card.stand_here: Stand in Angel Square, at the foot of the column, and look up at the angel with its raised trumpet. Keep the café fronts and buildings around the edges of your shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the angel, its column and the square together. Standing close and want the café fronts in too? Try 0.5x. For the angel and trumpet against the sky, use 2x or more, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the angel, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't wash out the bronze.
card.best_time: Go at sunset, when the bronze wings catch the light. Skip 1 April if you want the square to yourself, because it's the district's independence day and it gets busy.
card.selfie_here: Head to the wall of constitution plaques on Paupio gatvė, a short walk from the angel square. Bloggers call it the district's top selfie spot, so use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the wall of languages over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by in Angel Square, at the junction of Užupio gatvė and Malūnų gatvė, to shoot you at the foot of the column while they step back so the angel fits above you.
card.rules_and_safety: Užupis is a place where people live, so keep your voice down and use judgement around private courtyards. Street photos are fine, but ask first before photographing inside open galleries or studios.
card.challenge: Find Article 12, "A dog has the right to be a dog", on the wall, then strike your best trumpet-blowing pose in front of the angel.
card.good_to_know: The angel stands on an 8.5 m column and was unveiled on 1 April 2002. Its sculptor, Romas Vilčiauskas, also made the Užupis Mermaid. The money for the angel came from selling miniature copies, and it's a symbol of the district's revival.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Angel Square, at the foot of the column, and look up at the angel with its raised trumpet. Keep the café fronts and buildings around the edges of your shot.

card.hook: Most people crane their necks to look up at Vilnius Cathedral. From the Three Crosses hill, you get to look down on it, with the whole Old Town roofscape spread out beside it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the terrace by the Three Crosses monument, on the hill in Kalnų park. The cathedral lies to the west, so face west and look down across the Vilnia valley.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch the valley, the rooftops and the cathedral together. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the cathedral closer. Zoom 0.5x makes it tiny, so save it for shots where the sky and the hill are the star.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the cathedral on one of the third lines with rooftops below and sky above, then tap the cathedral and slide darker a touch so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Guides say the morning light is better from here. Sunrise and sunset are also recommended, and sunset is the classic time.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, head down to Cathedral Square and try the open paving near the cathedral's steps, which one guide calls wide open for group selfies. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and keep the cathedral over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a full-facade shot of you, ask a passer-by to stand across Cathedral Square facing the cathedral's front while you stand in front of it, and pick a spot where the whole facade is visible.
card.rules_and_safety: The hill and Kalnų park are a free public space, but check the official site before you go for the cathedral itself and the Gediminas Tower, which may have access rules or a fee. Photography is generally allowed inside the cathedral, but look for posted signs or ask church officials, especially about flash. If you climb the Bell Tower, wear sturdy shoes because the steps can get narrow.
card.challenge: Take three frames of the same view at zoom 1x, 2x and 5x, then see which one makes you say 'ooh' first.
card.good_to_know: The first documented cathedral on this site was consecrated in 1388. The calm, strict Neoclassical look you see today comes from a rebuild that began in the early 1780s under Laurynas Gucevičius and was finished in 1801. It's one of Lithuania's most important religious buildings.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the terrace by the Three Crosses monument, on the hill in Kalnų park. The cathedral lies to the west, so face west and look down across the Vilnia valley.

card.hook: Picture a tall, skinny gate squeezed between pastel buildings, with a little chapel window peeking out just above the arch. That's the Gate of Dawn, and it's a lot more photogenic than its size suggests.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on Aušros Vartų gatvė, in the lane in front of the gate. Don't stand right under the arch, because that gives a weaker picture. Face the gate so the arch, the window and the vault above it all fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 2x to 5x from up the street, which squeezes the lane so the arch and window fill the frame. Zoom 1x works too if you want more of the buildings in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the arch up with the centre so the buildings on both sides balance, then tap the arch and slide it a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the painted details.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the tour groups arrive. One guide says late afternoon light suits the chapel best.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the cobbled Aušros Vartų Street with the gate right behind you. Use the front camera and try zoom 0.5x to fit more of the gate in. For a second spot, go to the Baroque Basilian Gate, which has the Gate of Dawn in the background.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand about 80 m back up the cobbled lane, where the width of the street lets the gate sit between the pastel buildings, while you stand near the gate.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography isn't allowed inside the chapel, or during services. Stay on the pavement, not in the road, and keep entrances clear. Ask before taking close portraits of people, and be extra careful around worshippers.
card.challenge: Look at the outside of the gate and find the old firing openings, then get one in your photo.
card.good_to_know: The Gate of Dawn was built between 1503 and 1514 as one of nine gates in Vilnius's old city wall. It's the only one still standing. The small chapel above the arch holds a 17th-century painting of the Virgin Mary, and both Lithuanians and Poles hold the place dear.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on Aušros Vartų gatvė, in the lane in front of the gate. Don't stand right under the arch, because that gives a weaker picture. Face the gate so the arch, the window and the vault above it all fit in one frame.

card.hook: Here's a plot twist: the palace isn't the star up close, the whole Old Town is. From the hill above, it's one big pale building tucked in among the roofs and the cathedral, and that's what makes the shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on Trijų kryžių kalnas, the lookout on the hill above the Old Town, to the east of the palace. Face down over the Old Town and look for the big pale building near the cathedral.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the whole Old Town panorama. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the palace among its neighbours, and use 1x if you want something in the middle.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper line so the roofs fill most of the picture.
card.best_time: Go at golden hour, when one guide says the city gets a magical glow. Pick a clear day if you can, because you'll see far more detail.
card.selfie_here: Head down to the palace facade beside Vilnius Cathedral on Cathedral Square. Use the front camera at 0.5x and stand at the palace front so it fills the background behind your shoulder. The inner courtyard, with its historic walls behind you, is another good backdrop, and one guide suggests going early for soft light and fewer people.
card.ask_someone: On Cathedral Square next to the palace front by the cathedral, ask a passer-by to stand on the square and frame the palace with you in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos without flash are generally fine inside for personal use, but check the signs or ask staff. The courtyard may be inside the paid museum, so check access before you go.
card.challenge: Try to fit the cathedral, the palace and at least ten rooftops into one wide shot, then zoom in and see if you can catch just the palace.
card.good_to_know: The palace was first built in the 15th century for the rulers of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and was pulled down in 1801. Work on a new palace on the same site began in 2002, took 16 years and finished in 2018. The rebuilt palace is in a Renaissance style. Check the official site to see whether the hill is free and whether the palace interior is ticketed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Trijų kryžių kalnas, the lookout on the hill above the Old Town, to the east of the palace. Face down over the Old Town and look for the big pale building near the cathedral.

card.hook: Some buildings don't need a filter to look serious, and this one proves it. The solid, formal frontage of the old KGB headquarters does the talking before you've even taken the shot.
card.stand_here: Head to the Museum of Occupations and Freedom Fights, where the phone icon on the map sits right beside the building. Face the frontage and start with the whole thing in view.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view. If the whole frontage won't fit from the pavement, drop to 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for windows and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them, so the walls stand straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Go in soft, even daylight, like a bright overcast day, which suits the stonework. A quieter time of day also helps keep the entrance clear of people.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the edge of Lukiškės Square, the side facing the museum, and use your front camera with the building behind your shoulder. Try 0.5x if your front camera has it, so more of the facade fits in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Gediminas Avenue pavement opposite the building, facing the front, so the whole facade fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working courthouse and archive as well as a museum, so be considerate of people coming and going. Keep your photos respectful of the place and of anyone near the entrance. Shoot the outside from the public pavement, and check the official site for visiting arrangements.
card.challenge: Get one shot of the whole frontage, then one close-up of a single window or doorway where the stonework fills the frame.
card.good_to_know: The building dates from 1890 and was completed as the court of the Vilna Governorate. From 1944 until independence was re-established in 1991 it was the KGB's base, with offices, a prison and an interrogation centre. The museum was established in 1992 and took its current name in 2018.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the Museum of Occupations and Freedom Fights, where the phone icon on the map sits right beside the building. Face the frontage and start with the whole thing in view.

card.hook: Napoleon supposedly saw this church in 1812 and wished he could carry it home to Paris in the palm of his hand. Stand in front of that red brick and you'll see why.
card.stand_here: Head to Bernardinų sodas, the garden across the street from the church facade. The church is to the west, about 4 minutes on foot, so walk towards the brick towers and face the church from the garden.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to show the church rising above the trees. Switch to 0.5x if the towers get cut off, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the brick patterns and the top of the facade.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the church, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the red brick stays rich.
card.best_time: Soft daylight suits the brick colour best. In summer the church is said to be lit at night, so try night mode then and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the grass and small square in front of the church (Onos aikštė) with your back to the facade. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and let the towers rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand at the garden entrance across Pilies Street while you stand in front of the church, so the whole facade and both towers fit behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside the church is restricted and flash isn't allowed, so check the official site for opening hours before you go. The outside is fine to photograph from public streets and the garden.
card.challenge: Keep your phone upright and use the gridlines to get both towers perfectly straight, with the garden trees filling the bottom of the frame.
card.good_to_know: The present church went up in 1495-1500, and its outside has changed very little since. The builders used 33 different kinds of clay brick, which is why the walls look so textured. It stands right beside the much larger Church of St Francis and St Bernardine, and the two make a great pair.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Bernardinų sodas, the garden across the street from the church facade. The church is to the west, about 4 minutes on foot, so walk towards the brick towers and face the church from the garden.

card.hook: Here's a twist: from the garden at the bottom of the hill, the three famous crosses aren't the star. The star is the Old Town roofline peeking over the trees, and the crosses are a quick, steep climb away.
card.stand_here: Start in Bernardinų sodas, on the raised section near the Vilnelė river bank at the foot of the hill. Look over the mature garden trees to the Old Town roofline, with the wooded hill rising behind it.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x here and let the tree branches frame the roofline. Up on the hilltop deck, switch to zoom 0.5x to fit the crosses and the Old Town together, and use 2x to 5x to pick out spires and rooftops.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the crosses, then slide the brightness a little darker so the white crosses and bright sky keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon towards sunset, because the hill's view faces west. If you stay on after dusk, switch to night mode and rest your phone against a railing or tree to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the viewing platform beneath the Three Crosses and stand at the terrace railing. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the crosses over your shoulder, with the Old Town spread out beyond.
card.rules_and_safety: The climb is steep, and the steps and paths can be slippery when wet and icy in winter, so wear proper footwear. The paths are also unlit, so bring a torch if you stay until dusk. The hill is in a public park, but check the official site for access changes or path closures before you go.
card.challenge: Crouch down on the hilltop deck until the three white crosses stand against the sky, then see if you can still spot Gediminas Tower in the background.
card.good_to_know: Wooden crosses stood on this hill from the early 17th century, and legend links it to Franciscan friars who were put to death here. The wood rotted and the crosses collapsed in 1869. A concrete monument by Antoni Wiwulski followed in 1916, was pulled down in 1950, and was rebuilt in 1989 by Stanislovas Kuzma, 1.8 metres taller than the 1916 version.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start in Bernardinų sodas, on the raised section near the Vilnelė river bank at the foot of the hill. Look over the mature garden trees to the Old Town roofline, with the wooded hill rising behind it.

card.hook: Right in the middle of Vilnius's main square there's a tile where visitors step on, spin around three times and make a wish. Behind it, a huge cathedral and a bell tower that stands apart from it, and it all fits in one phone shot.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject: on the Stebuklas tile in the middle of Cathedral Square. Face the cathedral so the facade and bell tower sit behind the tile.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the cathedral, bell tower and tile together. Go to 0.5x if the facade won't fit or you want more of the square. For a tighter shot of the bell tower, try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the tile in the lower third with the cathedral and bell tower above it, then tap the cathedral facade and nudge brighter or darker if the sky or stonework looks off.
card.best_time: Golden hour is the one to aim for, with the cathedral glowing behind the tile. Earlier in the morning is also likely to be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the Stebuklas tile at the heart of the square, with the cathedral behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the cathedral over your shoulder, ideally at golden hour.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to frame you on the tile in the square, with the front of the cathedral in view behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The bell tower and Gediminas Tower may be ticketed, so check the official sites before you go. If you climb the bell tower, the steps can get narrow, so wear sturdy shoes.
card.challenge: Get a shot of a friend mid-spin on the tile, with the cathedral and bell tower still easy to recognise behind them.
card.good_to_know: The square was laid out in the 19th century, when the cathedral was being rebuilt. Red granite strips in the paving mark the outline of the old castle fortifications. The bell tower stands a few yards from the cathedral, which is unusual outside Italy, and its oldest underground section dates from the 13th century.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject: on the Stebuklas tile in the middle of Cathedral Square. Face the cathedral so the facade and bell tower sit behind the tile.

card.hook: Pilies Street is only a short stroll, but it feels like a market, a parade route and a souvenir hunt all squeezed into one lane. Amber glints from the stalls and linen flutters in the doorways, so there's something to point your phone at in every direction.
card.stand_here: Stand near Pilies g., about 65 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Walk a few steps closer if you want the street itself to fill the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view down the street. Tap 0.5x to squeeze in the buildings on both sides plus the stalls, then try 2x for close-ups like amber jewellery, linen or a stall display.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, run the street down the centre line so the buildings lead the eye in, and tuck a stall or shop front into one corner for depth.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually the quietest, so that's your best bet for a clean view of the street. Later in the day it gets lively, which is great for stalls and people, and festival days like the Kaziukas Fair are colourful but properly crowded.
card.selfie_here: Head to the cobbled stretch just below Cathedral Square, use the front camera at 0.5x, and turn so Gediminas Tower sits small in the distance over your shoulder. For something different, one walking route praises the courtyard of the Sidabrynas antique shop, behind the big wooden gate on Pilies Street, as one of the prettiest on the street.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd, then fire off a few frames in a row and see if you can catch a stall owner mid-smile in the corner of your shot.
card.good_to_know: Pilies Street means "Castle Street" and links Cathedral Square with Town Hall Square. It's where many of the city's festival processions pass, and the Kaziukas Fair brings folk artists from all over Lithuania. The House of the Signatories, where the Declaration of Independence was signed on 16 February 1918, is linked to the street too.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Pilies g., about 65 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Walk a few steps closer if you want the street itself to fill the frame.

card.hook: The Town Hall is the calm, formal one in a square that is rarely quiet. That makes it a lovely backdrop for whatever is happening in front of it.
card.stand_here: Stand near Rotušės a., at the phone icon, about 55 m north-east of the Town Hall, and face south-west. You'll be looking back at the building across open ground.
card.zoom: Start at 1x. If you can't fit the full width of the building in, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x for details like the roofline and the portico.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the walls up with them, so the building stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people in the square. Soft evening light is also pleasant on the building, and if the façade is lit, night mode can give you a good shot after dark.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the open square directly in front of the Town Hall, ideally early in the morning when it's empty, and use the front camera with the building behind you. For a different angle, go to the marble fountain on the far side of the square, near the Vilnius compass, so you've got water in front and the Town Hall in the frame. Try 0.5x to fit more of it in.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is an open public space. If you want to visit the cellars, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot with a few people walking through to show how big the square is, then a second with the square almost to yourself. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The Town Hall was first mentioned in 1432 and began as a Gothic building. It was rebuilt many times, and the neoclassical version you see now was designed by Laurynas Gucevičius in 1799 and is unchanged since. The Gothic cellars survive and can be visited. The square hosts Kaziukas Fair, the main Christmas tree, concerts and national celebrations.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Rotušės a., at the phone icon, about 55 m north-east of the Town Hall, and face south-west. You'll be looking back at the building across open ground.

card.hook: Crouch down by the rose beds in Bernardine Garden and the fountain pops up behind the flowers, like it's been waiting for its close-up.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject: the main rose garden in the central part of the park. Face the fountain, so the rose beds fill the foreground and the water sits behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole scene of beds and fountain, then try 1x for a more natural look. Go to 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the fountain jets or a single rose bed.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the fountain on one third, and crouch a little so the roses sit above the lawn and path.
card.best_time: The beds look best in the flowering season. Come in the evening for the lit fountain: on a warm-season weekday the music and light show runs from 9 pm to 10 pm, but check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Visitors say the landscaped areas just inside the main gate, on both sides of the path, make a lovely selfie backdrop. For water and greenery, try the Vilnelė riverbank near the ponds. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold it a little low so the garden fits behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a public park. For fountain times and any events or exhibitions, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get low and take one shot where a curve of roses leads your eye straight to the fountain, then show it off as your 'professional garden photographer' moment.
card.good_to_know: The garden covers over 9 hectares and sits between the Gediminas Tower and the Bernardine Monastery. Bernardine monks laid it out after being invited to Vilnius in 1469. It was closed in 1864, rebuilt later, destroyed in the Second World War, then rebuilt in the Soviet period and again in 2013.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject: the main rose garden in the central part of the park. Face the fountain, so the rose beds fill the foreground and the water sits behind them.

card.hook: Picture one long, dead-straight street where every building on both sides seems to point at a cathedral. That's Gediminas Avenue, and it's the main street of Vilnius.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement of Gediminas Avenue (Gedimino prospektas), about 1 km west of the subject, and face east so the street runs away from you toward Vilnius Cathedral. Pick a spot with a clear line down the street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view down the avenue. Try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the facades on both sides, or zoom 2x if your phone has it to bring the Cathedral a bit closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the buildings so the street stays nice and straight.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter. In the evening part of the avenue is closed to traffic, so it's calmer to shoot, and the low western sun should light up the buildings in front of you.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and stand with the avenue stretching out behind your shoulder so the street fits in. Keep your arm low and tilt the phone up a little to catch more buildings.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an open public street, so keep to the pavement and take care at crossings.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the people and traffic, then grab one shot where the whole street looks like it belongs only to you.
card.good_to_know: The avenue was built in 1836 and has had several names since, including St. George Avenue, Stalin Avenue and Lenin Avenue. It has carried its present name since 1989. The section from the Cathedral to Vincas Kudirka Square was rebuilt before 2003, and more than 100 new trees were planted along it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement of Gediminas Avenue (Gedimino prospektas), about 1 km west of the subject, and face east so the street runs away from you toward Vilnius Cathedral. Pick a spot with a clear line down the street.

card.hook: Look up above the door and you'll spot Mary standing on a cannon, which is not something you see on every church. The whole white Baroque building sits on a little hill, so it looks like it's showing off.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon near P. Vileišio g., about 150 m west of the church, and face east. From here the church and its hill should fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x here to get the whole facade and both towers in one shot. Then walk closer and try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the Mary-and-cannon relief and the tops of the towers.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white wall, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the pale stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Soft morning light, late afternoon or an evenly overcast day suits a white building best. Strong midday sun makes the walls glare.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold your phone a bit low and tilt it up so the towers rise behind your shoulder. Step back far enough that both towers fit in.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working Roman Catholic church, so opening times, dress expectations and photography rules inside may apply. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Zoom in to 5x and find Mary on her cannon, then take one shot with her perfectly centred between the towers.
card.good_to_know: Jan Zaor of Kraków designed the church. Building began on 29 June 1668 and the main work finished in 1676, paid for by Michał Kazimierz Pac to mark a victory over the Muscovites, who had occupied Vilnius for six years. Inside, around 2,000 white stucco figures cover the walls and ceilings.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the phone icon near P. Vileišio g., about 150 m west of the church, and face east. From here the church and its hill should fit in one frame.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names an exterior selfie spot or a named place where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the church behind them, so I have listed none. The pages name only interior features (the ceiling frescoes, the crypt, and the view down the main aisle to the altar) and Gediminas Hill, which is not this landmark. Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vilnius_Sts_Peter_et_Paul_Church_01.jpg) gives a camera position of 54.694093, 25.303923, but no name, so I did not use it. The unknown.lt page (https://www.unknown.lt/en/location/st-peter-paul-church-vilnius) gives coordinates of 54.6906, 25.2964, which differ from the position you supplied. Pages also disagree on interior photography: airial.travel says it is generally allowed, while thingstodoinvilnius.com says it costs an extra small fee. No page mentions selfie sticks or tripods, so no rules are listed. Sources checked include airial.travel, wanderlog.com, unknown.lt, thingstodoinvilnius.com, Wikipedia, Wikimedia Commons, and yomadic.com.

card.hook: Most streets hang a sign and leave it there. Literatų Street covers its walls in around 200 tiny tributes to writers, and you'll be hunting for your favourite within seconds.
card.stand_here: Stand on Literatų gatvė, in the middle of the street, facing the plaque-covered walls. From the Old Town of Vilnius, it's about 1 minute on foot to the north-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the narrow lane and the whole wall fit in one frame. Switch to 1x for little groups of plaques, then 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a single plaque.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the wall lined up with the edge of the frame, so everything looks nice and straight.
card.best_time: Go early in the day, or whenever the lane is quiet, so nobody walks in front of your wall. The lane can be shady, so hold your phone steady with both hands.
card.selfie_here: Try the main plaque wall, just along from where Literatų gatvė meets Rusų gatvė. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the patchwork of plaques behind your shoulder. You can also try the start of the street, by the building with three Mickiewicz plaques in Lithuanian, Russian and Polish.
card.rules_and_safety: The street is pedestrian-only. If it's busy with selfie-takers, snap quickly so others can read the plaques, and ask before taking a close photo of a stranger.
card.challenge: Find two plaques that clash in colour or material, step in close and fill the whole frame with just those two.
card.good_to_know: The first plaques went up in 2009, when Vilnius was European Capital of Culture, and there are now around 200. Literatų means 'of the literati', maybe thanks to the printing houses and bookshops that once stood here. Or it may come from the poet Adam Mickiewicz, who lived here briefly in 1823.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Literatų gatvė, in the middle of the street, facing the plaque-covered walls. From the Old Town of Vilnius, it's about 1 minute on foot to the north-east.

card.hook: Two tall towers, a front covered in carved decoration, and a little square where you can stand back and take it all in. St. Catherine's is the kind of church that makes you stop mid-stroll and reach for your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand in S. Moniuškos skveras, the small square right beside the church, and face the front of the church. You'll look straight across at the twin towers, with the Moniuszko bust close by.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit both towers and the whole front in one frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the pediments and tower tops.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the towers up with the vertical lines, and hold the phone level so the walls don't lean inwards.
card.best_time: A soft, overcast day suits the pale stonework nicely. Early in the day the square is usually quieter too.
card.selfie_here: Try the square in front of the church, on the Vilniaus gatvė side. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the church behind you over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an active church and concert venue, so check opening hours before you go if you'd like to see inside.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of both towers, then find the fanciest bit of carving up high and zoom in on it like a detective.
card.good_to_know: Jan Karol Chodkiewicz, Hetman of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, founded the church in 1618 for Benedictine nuns. After the Great Fire of 1737, architect Johann Christoph Glaubitz gave it its current look, with five-storey towers and ornate pediments. It was a warehouse in Soviet times, went back to the Vilnius Archdiocese in 2002, and now hosts cultural events too.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in S. Moniuškos skveras, the small square right beside the church, and face the front of the church. You'll look straight across at the twin towers, with the Moniuszko bust close by.

selfie_research.notes: Weak evidence. No page I found calls any spot the best selfie spot, and none names a place where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole church. The only named spot is the square in front of the church, taken from a single TripAdvisor photo caption, so the selfie spot is an inference. Wikimedia Commons lists photographer positions only as coordinates (for example 54.68122, 25.28121, heading 337.5 degrees), which are not named places, so I left them out. The Audiala guide says photography is generally allowed outside performances, but it states no selfie stick or tripod rule, so rules is empty. Opening hours vary because the church is used for concerts and events, and one review says it was closed when visited. Confirm access and whether the square is a good frame before going.

card.hook: Here's a church that looks like a little fortress, and it's rising straight out of the Vilnia riverbank. Best of all, the bridge gives you a front-row view of it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Užupio tiltas, on the Užupis side of the Vilnia riverbank, and face north across the water to the cathedral. Let the bridge sit in the foreground to frame your shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the cathedral across the river. Zoom 0.5x if you want more of the bridge and riverbank, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the facade and its details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep the cathedral in the upper two-thirds, and use the bridge as a leading edge at the bottom or side of the frame.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light is softer and there are fewer people on the bridge.
card.selfie_here: Try the Užupis footbridge, close to the cathedral. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the cathedral rise over your shoulder. The riverside terrace of Užupio kavinė is another spot to try, but check on the spot that the cathedral fits behind you.
card.ask_someone: For a photo of you with the cathedral, ask a passer-by at the corner where Maironio and Malūnų streets meet, by the bridge over the Vilnia, where the cathedral is in view.
card.rules_and_safety: The cathedral is a working place of worship, though the view from the bridge is from a public place. Check the official site before you go if you want to visit inside.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with the whole bridge in it, then step in with the zoom for a facade close-up. Bonus points if no stranger wanders into either one!
card.good_to_know: The cathedral's story goes back to 1346, when it was built for Uliana of Tver, the Orthodox wife of Grand Duke Algirdas. The university once used it as a library and an anatomical theatre. The look you see today mostly comes from the rebuilding of 1865 to 1868, which imitated medieval Georgian architecture. It was renovated in 1998.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Užupio tiltas, on the Užupis side of the Vilnia riverbank, and face north across the water to the cathedral. Let the bridge sit in the foreground to frame your shot.

The found pages name no explicit selfie spot with the cathedral behind the visitor; the two selfie spots are inferred from view descriptions, so check them on the ground. The ask-someone spot is from a photo caption, not a tip for passers-by. Sources give different names for the building (Dormition, Assumption, Holy Mother of God). card.hook: You're in a narrow Old Town street, craning your neck, and a white bell tower keeps rising past where you thought it would stop. That's St John's, and it's 69 metres of pure photo bait.
card.stand_here: Stand on Šv. Jono gatvė, the small side street off Pilies gatvė. The church is a short step to the north, so face the tower rising from the street with the church alongside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the tower and church together in the tight street. If you can step back, try 1x for a more natural shape, and zoom 2x to 5x for the top of the tower (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower's edges up with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the sky is bright but the street isn't crowded; early morning is usually quieter. A bright overcast day gives soft, even light that suits the pale tower.
card.selfie_here: Head into the Grand Courtyard of Vilnius University and stand facing away from the church's main façade. Use the front camera so the façade and bell tower sit behind you, and try 0.5x if you want more tower in the shot.
card.ask_someone: In the Grand Courtyard, hand your phone to a passer-by, stand with the church's main façade and bell tower behind you, and ask them to shoot from the courtyard side.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship, so dress modestly and be quiet if you go in. The bell tower has 193 wooden steps or a lift, so think twice if you hate heights. It's closed from roughly late October to April, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Get the tower standing perfectly straight on the gridlines with no wires or signs poking in. A few steps left or right usually does it.
card.good_to_know: At 69 metres, the tower is the tallest building in the Old Town. A Gothic parish church was finished here in the 1420s, and after a fire in 1737 the architect Johann Christoph Glaubitz gave the front its flowing, wavy Vilnius Baroque lines. The Jesuits received the church in 1571, and it still hosts services in Lithuanian and concerts.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Šv. Jono gatvė, the small side street off Pilies gatvė. The church is a short step to the north, so face the tower rising from the street with the church alongside it.
